desc:
A circular track has n cells numbered 0 to n - 1 clockwise; after cell n - 1 comes cell 0 again. An arc [start, length] covers length consecutive cells clockwise, beginning with cell start: the cells start, start + 1, ... taken modulo n. An arc with length = n covers the whole track.

Return the minimum number of arcs from the list that together cover every cell of the track, or -1 if that is impossible.

n = 10, arcs = [[0, 4], [3, 4], [6, 5], [8, 3]]  ->  3
n = 6,  arcs = [[0, 2], [3, 2]]                  ->  -1

In the first example the arcs [0, 4] (cells 0-3), [3, 4] (cells 3-6) and [6, 5] (cells 6, 7, 8, 9, 0) cover all ten cells. In the second, cells 2 and 5 are never covered.
constraints: arcs[i] = [start, length] with 0 ≤ start < n and 1 ≤ length ≤ n
hints: On a straight line this is the classic greedy: from the covered prefix, jump to the farthest end among arcs starting at or before it. What breaks on a circle?

The circle has no left end. But some arc of an optimal answer starts at some cell; if you know which one, unroll the circle there and the line greedy applies. Duplicate every arc one lap further (start + n) so wrapping arcs become ordinary.

Precompute g[x] = the farthest end reachable with arcs starting at or before x on the doubled line. For every possible starting cell s count the jumps needed to get from s to s + n. Doing that naively costs too much, so use binary lifting on g and take the minimum over all starting cells.
editorial: Take an optimal cover and look at one of its arcs, which starts at cell s. Cut the circle at s and unroll it to the line s .. s + n. Add a copy of each arc shifted by n so that arcs that wrap around the cut appear as ordinary intervals on the doubled line 0 .. 2n. Now we need the fewest intervals that cover [s, s + n), which the greedy jump solves: from covered boundary x, the next boundary is g[x], the largest end among intervals with start ≤ x. We only need to try cuts at starting cells of arcs, as at least one arc of any minimal cover starts there.

Running the jump greedy separately from each of up to n starting cells could take O(n) jumps each. Because g is a fixed function, precompute up[j][x], the boundary after 2j jumps, and for each start s take the largest jumps that stay below s + n, then one more jump; if it does not reach s + n the chain is stuck. The minimum over all starts is the answer, or -1. Time O((n + m) log n) with m arcs, space O(n log n). Every chain of k jumps is a cover by at most k distinct arcs, so no start gives an impossible result, and the best start gives the optimum.
